name: 161 Gallowgate
body: Douglass lodged for roughly three months above William Smeal's grocery shop — his main base while touring Scotland. He returned regularly to collect shipments of his Narrative to sell at lectures for half a crown.
note: The original building is gone, replaced c.1880. One Glasgow Life source lists the address as '38 Gallowgate' instead — likely a historic renumbering, but unresolved.

name: City Hall, Candleriggs
body: His primary Glasgow venue. First lecture here drew 1,500 people; a later meeting drew 2,500. Opened 1841 as a new civic hall — survives today as City Halls, a working concert venue.
linkLabel: Read: 'An Account of American Slavery' (15 Jan 1846)

name: City Hall — Temperance meeting
body: A packed Scottish Temperance League meeting; doors opened at 6, Douglass spoke alongside Henry Vincent and Thomas Beggs across four and a half hours, ending near midnight.
linkLabel: Read: 'Intemperance Viewed in Connection With Slavery'

name: City Hall — Free Church protest
body: Likely his most consequential Glasgow speech — a direct attack on the Free Church of Scotland's American donations, fueling the 'Send Back the Money' campaign. Delivered alongside Henry Clarke Wright and George Thompson.
linkLabel: Read: 'The Free Church Alliance with Man-Stealers'

name: City Hall — return with Garrison
body: Delivered after Douglass returned to Glasgow in autumn with William Lloyd Garrison. Venue inferred from context — not explicitly confirmed as City Hall in this source.
linkLabel: Read: 'Slavery, The Evangelical Alliance, and The Free Church'

name: Assembly Rooms, Ingram Street
body: Douglass addressed the Glasgow Female Emancipation Society here on both dates, ahead of larger evening meetings at City Hall. No surviving full transcript found.
note: Building demolished 1892. Its 1796 facade survives — relocated in 1991 to Glasgow Green as the McLennan Arch, over half a mile from the original site.

name: Eagle Temperance Hotel, York Street
body: Douglass and Garrison addressed a breakfast gathering of 'seventy friends' here before departing by train for Kilmarnock. No surviving transcript found.
note: Site now occupied by an office block on Atlantic Quay.

name: Trades Hall, Glassford Street
body: A Robert Adam building (1791–94), still standing essentially unchanged and used by other abolitionist lecturers in this era (Moses Roper, William Wells Brown, the Crafts, Sarah Parker Remond).
note: No source found confirming Douglass himself spoke here — likely a building he knew, but not verified as a lecture site for him specifically.
source: Frederick Douglass in Britain and Ireland (frederickdouglassinbritain.com)

name: Terminus, Glasgow–Ayr Railway (Bridge Street)
body: Douglass first arrived in Glasgow on the evening of 10 January via a train from Ardrossan, passing through this station repeatedly during the year.
note: Station closed 1905; site now a restaurant.

name: Terminus, Glasgow–Edinburgh Railway (Queen Street)
body: Departure and arrival point for trips to Edinburgh — four trains daily, a two-and-a-half-hour journey.
note: Station substantially rebuilt since; none of the 1840s structure remains.

name: Edinburgh — Music Hall / Waterloo Rooms
note: Photo shows Edinburgh's Old College, not the Music Hall/Waterloo Rooms building itself — included for local context pending a photo of the actual site.
body: A busy May Day: a public breakfast and a Ladies' Emancipation Society meeting at the Waterloo Rooms, then an evening address to 2,000 people at the Music Hall on George Street.

name: Perth, City Hall
body: Several addresses delivered over about a week, alongside Henry C. Wright and James Buffum, to large and attentive audiences per contemporary press coverage.
source: Perthshire Constitutional, 28 Jan 1846 (repr. Liberator) via bulldozia.com

name: Dundee — soiree
body: An evening event held in honor of Douglass, Wright, and Buffum, reported at length in the Dundee Courier the following week.

name: Paisley — Rev. Nisbet's church & Exchange Rooms
body: Multiple visits over the year, including a temperance address and a crowded meeting later moved to Paisley's largest church after tickets were being resold above face value.

name: Ayr — Relief Church, Cathcart Street
body: Douglass named his former enslaver, Thomas Auld, directly in a speech here, detailing the damage done to his family.

name: Kilmarnock
body: Confirmed stop on the itinerary, reached by train after a breakfast address in Glasgow.

name: Bonhill / Vale of Leven
body: First of several meetings in the Vale of Leven area.

name: Duntocher
body: Dated only by inference: Douglass referenced having recently spoken in Duntocher during an April 6 Paisley speech, and was confirmed elsewhere on April 3 — narrowing it to this window, but no direct contemporary report of the meeting itself has been found.

name: Aberdeen, Arbroath, Montrose, Greenock, Kirkcaldy
body: Named by Douglass himself as tour stops ('the people are with us in Arbroath, Dundee, Aberdeen, Montrose, Greenock, Glasgow') and by secondary sources, but specific venues and dates for each have not yet been individually verified here.

name: Hawick, Galashiels, Coldstream (Borders)
body: Sometimes listed online as Douglass stops, but a specialist source explicitly states this Borders tour was undertaken by his colleague Henry Clarke Wright alone — Douglass did not accompany him.
note: Included here specifically as a caution: this is a documented case of misattribution circulating in secondary sources.
